title: How long does a river table really take to cure?
excerpt: Resin is not a material that forgives being rushed. A single pour on a river table can take four to six weeks from first mix to final polish, because…

content.text: Resin is not a material that forgives being rushed. A single pour on a river table can take four to six weeks from first mix to final polish, because the resin has to cure in stages — a bulk fill for the deep sections, a levelling coat for the surface, and a finishing coat that carries the gloss. Trying to shortcut that sequence is the single most common cause of the cloudy patches and cracks a new studio's early pieces tend to carry.

Wood movement is the part most people underestimate when they first commission a river table. Kiln-dried teak still breathes with the seasons, expanding a fraction across the grain in humid months and contracting again in the dry season. A well-built river table leaves the resin free to flex at the wood joint rather than bonding it rigidly, which is why a slightly imperfect seam is often the sign of a piece built to last rather than one built to look flawless in a showroom.

Cleaning a cured resin surface is simpler than most owners expect, and also easier to get wrong. A soft microfibre cloth and lukewarm water lift dust and light marks without dulling the topcoat; anything abrasive — a scouring pad, a solvent-based cleaner — will scratch a surface that is, chemically, closer to glass than to varnished wood. Direct midday sun is the other enemy: UV exposure over months is what yellows an unstabilised resin, which is why every piece leaving the studio is mixed with a UV inhibitor rather than relying on placement alone.

Pigment behaves differently in resin than in paint, because resin is translucent by nature and a pigment is suspended in it rather than sitting on top of a surface. Mica powders catch light and shift colour as the viewing angle changes; alcohol inks bloom outward from the point they are dropped in, which is what gives an ocean-wave piece its characteristic feathered edges rather than a flat wash of blue. Getting a repeatable palette across a run of coasters or a set of trays takes far more trial pours than most commissions ever see, because the studio discards a batch rather than ship a colour that reads differently from the sample photograph.
